Movement models with ctmm

Source: vignettes/articles/ctmm_models.Rmd
ctmm_models.Rmd

The package ctmm implements continuous-time movement models, which describe how the locations of an animal are correlated in time. Tracking data are strongly autocorrelated (consecutive locations are close to each other), and methods that assume independent locations, such as conventional kernel density estimation (KDE), underestimate home ranges and their uncertainty. Continuous-time movement models account for this autocorrelation, and are the basis of methods such as autocorrelated kernel density estimation (AKDE, Fleming et al. 2015).

tidytracks provides an interface to ctmm that follows a simple, modular workflow:

  1. prepare a tibble of tracks in a projected coordinate reference system;
  2. fit a movement model to each track with ctmm_tt_fit(), which returns a table of models with one row per track, in the same order as the metadata;
  3. inspect and summarise the models (ctmm_tt_summary());
  4. use the models, together with the tracks, for further analyses, such as estimating home ranges with hr_tt_akde().

In this article, we follow the examples of the ctmm vignettes, using the same data, to show how this workflow fits with the rest of tidytracks.

library(tidytracks)
library(ctmm)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

The data

We use the GPS tracks of African buffalo (Syncerus caffer) from Kruger National Park, South Africa (Getz et al. 2007, Cross et al. 2016), which are also used in the ctmm vignettes (ctmm provides them as a list of telemetry objects, which can be converted to a tibble of tracks with mt_as_move2()). Fitting movement models to long tracks takes a few minutes per track, so, to keep this article quick to run, we use four of the six buffalo of the dataset: Cilla, Gabs and Mvubu, which share an area in the south of the park, and Pepper, whose GPS collar changed its sampling schedule (see below).

The tracks are stored in a CSV file, with one row per location: the id of the buffalo (buffalo_id), the time in UTC (date_time), and the longitude and latitude (lon and lat). The file also includes the sex and the age class of each buffalo (sex and age; they are all adult females). As these values are repeated for all the locations of a buffalo, tt_read_data() moves them to the metadata of the tibble of tracks:

buffalo_tt <- tt_read_data(
  events = "data/buffalo_tracks.csv",
  col_track_id = "buffalo_id",
  col_coords = c("lon", "lat"),
  col_date_time = "date_time"
)
buffalo_tt
#> A <move2> with `track_id_column` "buffalo_id" and `time_column` "date_time"
#> Containing 4 tracks lasting on average 147 days in a
#> Simple feature collection with 9820 features and 2 fields
#> Geometry type: POINT
#> Dimension:     XY
#> Bounding box:  xmin: 31.71643 ymin: -25.16421 xmax: 31.98769 ymax: -24.05847
#> Geodetic CRS:  WGS 84
#> First 10 features:
#>    buffalo_id           date_time                   geometry
#> 1       Cilla 2005-07-14 05:35:00 POINT (31.88776 -24.96738)
#> 2       Cilla 2005-07-14 07:35:00 POINT (31.85942 -24.94288)
#> 3       Cilla 2005-07-14 08:34:00 POINT (31.85512 -24.94914)
#> 4       Cilla 2005-07-14 09:35:00 POINT (31.85694 -24.95424)
#> 5       Cilla 2005-07-14 10:35:00 POINT (31.85977 -24.94735)
#> 6       Cilla 2005-07-14 11:34:00 POINT (31.84466 -24.93435)
#> 7       Cilla 2005-07-14 12:35:00    POINT (31.8441 -24.934)
#> 8       Cilla 2005-07-14 13:34:00 POINT (31.84463 -24.93442)
#> 9       Cilla 2005-07-14 14:35:00   POINT (31.857 -24.93371)
#> 10      Cilla 2005-07-14 15:35:00 POINT (31.86478 -24.93985)

show_meta(buffalo_tt)
#>   buffalo_id    sex   age
#> 1      Cilla female adult
#> 2       Gabs female adult
#> 3      Mvubu female adult
#> 4     Pepper female adult
ggplot() +
  geom_track_path(data = buffalo_tt, mapping = aes(colour = buffalo_id)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(31.6, 32, by = 0.2)) +
  labs(colour = "Buffalo")

Projecting the data

ctmm works with coordinates in a projected CRS, with units in metres. If we try to use data in longitude and latitude, we get an error:

buffalo_fit <- ctmm_tt_fit(buffalo_tt)
#> Error:
#> ! ctmm requires x to be in a projected coordinate reference system (not longitude/latitude); project x with `sf::st_transform()`, e.g. using the projection suggested by `crstools::suggest_crs(x)` for the area covered by the tracks

The package crstools can suggest an appropriate projection for the area covered by the tracks. For home ranges, where we are interested in areas, an equal-area projection is a good choice (the default of crstools::suggest_crs()):

library(crstools)
buffalo_crs <- suggest_crs(buffalo_tt, quiet = TRUE)
buffalo_crs$description
#> [1] "Transverse cylindrical equal-area"
buffalo_tt <- sf::st_transform(buffalo_tt, buffalo_crs$wkt)

Fitting movement models

ctmm_tt_fit() fits a continuous-time movement model to each track. By default (model = "auto"), it selects the best model for each track based on AICc (with ctmm::ctmm.select()): starting from the model suggested by the variogram of the track, generally a model with autocorrelated positions and velocities (Ornstein-Uhlenbeck foraging, OUF), it fits simpler models, such as models with autocorrelated positions only (Ornstein-Uhlenbeck, OU), with independent locations (IID), or with isotropic movement, until AICc no longer improves. Fitting can take a while for long tracks; ctmm prints the minimum sampling interval of each track as it reads it.

buffalo_fit <- ctmm_tt_fit(buffalo_tt)
#> Minimum sampling interval of 3 minutes in Cilla
#> Minimum sampling interval of 2 minutes in Gabs
#> Minimum sampling interval of 2 minutes in Mvubu
#> Minimum sampling interval of 3 minutes in Pepper
buffalo_fit
#> # A tibble: 4 × 9
#>   buffalo_id model        model_name         aicc dof_area n_events
#>   <fct>      <named list> <chr>             <dbl>    <dbl>    <int>
#> 1 Cilla      <ctmm>       OUF anisotropic 100360.    18.1      3527
#> 2 Gabs       <ctmm>       OUF anisotropic  55552.     4.30     1996
#> 3 Mvubu      <ctmm>       OUF anisotropic  73064.    13.8      2572
#> 4 Pepper     <ctmm>       OUF anisotropic  53671.    15.7      1725
#> # ℹ 3 more variables: t_start <dttm>, t_end <dttm>, fit_message <chr>

The result is a table with one row per track, in the same order as the metadata of the tibble of tracks (see show_meta()). Besides the fitted models (column model), the table includes the name of the selected model, its AICc, and the effective sample size for the home range area (dof_area), which is much smaller than the number of locations because of autocorrelation: tracks with few home range crossings provide little information on the home range, and lead to uncertain estimates.

The table has the same id column as the metadata (buffalo_id), so it can be joined with the metadata, for example to compare the models of individuals of different sex or age (here, all the buffalo are adult females):

show_meta(buffalo_tt) %>%
  left_join(
    select(buffalo_fit, buffalo_id, model_name, dof_area),
    by = "buffalo_id"
  )
#>   buffalo_id    sex   age      model_name  dof_area
#> 1      Cilla female adult OUF anisotropic 18.135827
#> 2       Gabs female adult OUF anisotropic  4.295612
#> 3      Mvubu female adult OUF anisotropic 13.848033
#> 4     Pepper female adult OUF anisotropic 15.657504

With candidates = TRUE, ctmm_tt_fit() also returns all the candidate models of each track, which is useful to inspect the model selection. Instead of selecting a model, we can also fit a given model to all tracks (e.g. model = "ouf"), or provide model templates created with ctmm::ctmm().

Checking the fit of the models

The models are standard ctmm objects, so we can use all the functions of ctmm to inspect them. A good way to check the fit of a model is to compare it with the empirical variogram of the track, which shows the average square distance between locations as a function of the time lag between them (see the ctmm vignette on variograms). To use ctmm functions on the data, we convert the tibble of tracks to a list of telemetry objects with mt_as_telemetry():

buffalo_tel <- mt_as_telemetry(buffalo_tt)
names(buffalo_tel)
#> [1] "Cilla"  "Gabs"   "Mvubu"  "Pepper"

We can now compute the empirical variogram of Cilla, the first buffalo, and extract its fitted model:

cilla_svf <- variogram(buffalo_tel$Cilla)
cilla_model <- buffalo_fit$model$Cilla

and plot them together, both at short time lags (where we see the autocorrelation of the velocity) and at long time lags (where the variogram levels off at the size of the home range):

plot(
  cilla_svf,
  CTMM = cilla_model,
  xlim = c(0, 12 %#% "hour"),
  level = c(0.5, 0.95)
)
title("Cilla: short lags")
plot(cilla_svf, CTMM = cilla_model, fraction = 0.65, level = c(0.5, 0.95))
title("Cilla: long lags")

Summarising the models

ctmm_tt_summary() extracts the parameters of the models, with their confidence intervals, as a table with one row per track. The parameters include the area of the home range of the model (area), the home range crossing time (tau_position), the time scale of the autocorrelation of the velocity (tau_velocity), and the root-mean-square speed (speed), which is a convenient measure of how fast the animal moves, but not its mean speed (see Going further):

buffalo_summary <- ctmm_tt_summary(buffalo_fit)
names(buffalo_summary)
#>  [1] "buffalo_id"        "model_name"        "dof_area"         
#>  [4] "area_low"          "area_est"          "area_high"        
#>  [7] "tau_position_low"  "tau_position_est"  "tau_position_high"
#> [10] "tau_velocity_low"  "tau_velocity_est"  "tau_velocity_high"
#> [13] "speed_low"         "speed_est"         "speed_high"       
#> [16] "diffusion_low"     "diffusion_est"     "diffusion_high"

Each parameter has three columns: the lower bound of its confidence interval (_low), its estimate (_est) and the upper bound (_high). Printing such a wide table is not very useful, as the columns that do not fit in the console are hidden.

To look at the parameters we are interested in, we can use transmute() from dplyr, which keeps only the columns that we list, and can modify them at the same time (it combines select() and mutate()).

Modifying the columns is useful here, as the values are units objects in SI units: areas are in square metres, time scales in seconds, and speeds in metres per second. For buffalo, which live in home ranges of hundreds of square kilometres and take days to cross them, these numbers are very large or very small, and hard to interpret. With units::set_units(), we can convert each column to a more intuitive unit, which is shown under the name of the column:

buffalo_summary %>%
  transmute(
    buffalo_id,
    model_name,
    area_est = units::set_units(area_est, "km^2"),
    tau_position_est = units::set_units(tau_position_est, "days"),
    speed_est = units::set_units(speed_est, "km/day")
  )
#> # A tibble: 4 × 5
#>   buffalo_id model_name      area_est tau_position_est speed_est
#>   <fct>      <chr>             [km^2]              [d]    [km/d]
#> 1 Cilla      OUF anisotropic     403.             7.51      14.1
#> 2 Gabs       OUF anisotropic     529.            18.2       13.7
#> 3 Mvubu      OUF anisotropic     405.             6.75      14.4
#> 4 Pepper     OUF anisotropic     774.            13.4       16.5

We did not save the result of transmute(), as it is only used to display the table: buffalo_summary still has all its columns, in SI units. We use the same approach to display the other tables in this article.

Autocorrelated kernel density estimation

The fitted models can be used to estimate home ranges with AKDE, which accounts for the autocorrelation of locations. hr_tt_akde() requires both the tibble of tracks and the table of models:

buffalo_akde <- hr_tt_akde(buffalo_tt, buffalo_fit)
#> Default grid size of 3 minutes chosen for bandwidth(...,fast=TRUE).
#> Default grid size of 2 minutes chosen for bandwidth(...,fast=TRUE).
#> Default grid size of 2 minutes chosen for bandwidth(...,fast=TRUE).
#> Default grid size of 3 minutes chosen for bandwidth(...,fast=TRUE).
buffalo_akde
#> # A tibble: 4 × 11
#>   buffalo_id method model_name     dof_area    xmin    ymin   xmax    ymax   res
#>   <chr>      <chr>  <chr>             <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 Cilla      akde   OUF anisotrop…    18.1  -27948. -2.82e6 29196. -2.66e6  279.
#> 2 Gabs       akde   OUF anisotrop…     4.30 -27948. -2.82e6 29196. -2.66e6  279.
#> 3 Mvubu      akde   OUF anisotrop…    13.8  -27948. -2.82e6 29196. -2.66e6  279.
#> 4 Pepper     akde   OUF anisotrop…    15.7  -27948. -2.82e6 29196. -2.66e6  279.
#> # ℹ 2 more variables: ud <named list>, ud_ctmm <named list>

The result is a table of utilisation distributions (UDs) of class hr_tt_ud_tbl, as returned by hr_tt_kde(), which can be used with the other hr_tt_ functions. The UDs are estimated on a grid shared by all tracks; by default, its resolution follows the default of ctmm, and its extent contains all the UDs. The table also includes the UDs as ctmm objects (column ud_ctmm), which can be used with the functions of ctmm.

autoplot(buffalo_akde)

The isopleths (i.e. the home ranges at given levels) can be obtained from the UDs with hr_tt_ud_iso(), as for the other methods to estimate home ranges. For AKDE, the table of isopleths also includes the confidence intervals of the area of each home range (area_low and area_high), which ctmm estimates from the ctmm UDs:

buffalo_iso <- hr_tt_ud_iso(buffalo_akde, levels = c(0.5, 0.95))

The same isopleths can be obtained directly by setting levels in hr_tt_akde(), which is convenient if we do not need the UDs (we do so below). To display the areas, we use transmute() as above. The table of isopleths is an sf object, whose geometry column is always kept by transmute(), so we first drop it with sf::st_drop_geometry():

buffalo_iso %>%
  sf::st_drop_geometry() %>%
  transmute(
    buffalo_id,
    level,
    area = units::set_units(area, "km^2"),
    area_low = units::set_units(area_low, "km^2"),
    area_high = units::set_units(area_high, "km^2")
  )
#> # A tibble: 8 × 5
#>   buffalo_id level   area area_low area_high
#>   <chr>      <dbl> [km^2]   [km^2]    [km^2]
#> 1 Cilla       0.5    89.3     52.9      135.
#> 2 Cilla       0.95  375.     223.       568.
#> 3 Gabs        0.5   129.      37.6      279.
#> 4 Gabs        0.95  502.     146.      1080.
#> 5 Mvubu       0.5    83.1     45.1      132.
#> 6 Mvubu       0.95  365.     198.       579.
#> 7 Pepper      0.5   158.      90.2      247.
#> 8 Pepper      0.95  756.     430.      1176.
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(
    data = filter(buffalo_iso, level == 0.95),
    mapping = aes(fill = buffalo_id),
    alpha = 0.4
  ) +
  geom_track_path(
    data = buffalo_tt,
    mapping = aes(colour = buffalo_id),
    linewidth = 0.1
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(31.6, 32, by = 0.2)) +
  labs(fill = "Buffalo", colour = "Buffalo")

AKDE versus KDE

To see the effect of accounting for autocorrelation, we can compare the AKDE home ranges with those estimated with conventional KDE (hr_tt_kde()), using the reference bandwidth for each buffalo. So that the two estimates are comparable, we estimate the KDE on the same grid as the AKDE, using the bounding box and resolution of the grid stored in the table of AKDE UDs (the grid is the same for all buffalo, so we take it from the first row):

buffalo_kde_iso <- hr_tt_kde(
  buffalo_tt,
  h = "h_ref_indiv",
  bbox = unlist(buffalo_akde[1, c("xmin", "ymin", "xmax", "ymax")]),
  res = buffalo_akde$res[1],
  levels = 0.95
)

To compare the two estimates, we first stack the 95% home ranges of the two methods in a single table with bind_rows(), which appends the rows of the second table to those of the first. Both tables have a column method ("akde" or "kde"), so we can still tell which method each row comes from. Columns that are only present in one of the tables (e.g. the confidence intervals area_low and area_high, which KDE does not provide) are filled with NA for the rows of the other table:

buffalo_hr_95 <- bind_rows(
  filter(buffalo_iso, level == 0.95),
  buffalo_kde_iso
)

We then reshape the table with tidyr::pivot_wider(), so that each buffalo is a row and each method a column. pivot_wider() uses all the columns that are not reshaped to identify the rows, and these differ between the two methods (e.g. h, the bandwidth, is only defined for KDE), so we first use transmute() to keep only the id of the buffalo, the method and the area:

buffalo_hr_95 %>%
  sf::st_drop_geometry() %>%
  transmute(buffalo_id, method, area = units::set_units(area, "km^2")) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = method, values_from = area)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 3
#>   buffalo_id   akde    kde
#>   <chr>      [km^2] [km^2]
#> 1 Cilla        375.   294.
#> 2 Gabs         502.   212.
#> 3 Mvubu        365.   243.
#> 4 Pepper       756.   614.

Conventional KDE, which ignores the autocorrelation of the locations, gives smaller home ranges for all buffalo, and no measure of the uncertainty of the estimates. The difference is largest for Gabs, whose track has the fewest independent observations of the home range (the lowest dof_area, see above).

Irregular sampling

The tracks of some buffalo are sampled irregularly: Pepper, for example, was sampled every hour at the start of the deployment, and every two hours afterwards, because of a malfunction of the GPS collar. With weights = TRUE, hr_tt_akde() weights the locations to correct for the over-representation of the periods sampled more frequently (Fleming et al. 2018). This is slower, so here we only use it for Pepper:

pepper_tt <- filter_by_meta(buffalo_tt, buffalo_id == "Pepper")
pepper_iso <- bind_rows(
  uniform = hr_tt_akde(pepper_tt, buffalo_fit, levels = 0.95),
  weighted = hr_tt_akde(pepper_tt, buffalo_fit, levels = 0.95, weights = TRUE),
  .id = "weights"
)
#> Default grid size of 3 minutes chosen for bandwidth(...,fast=TRUE).
#> Default grid size of 3 minutes chosen for bandwidth(...,fast=TRUE).

Here, the two tables have the same columns, so we name them in bind_rows() (uniform and weighted), and use .id to add a column weights with the name of the table each row comes from. We can then compare the areas:

pepper_iso %>%
  sf::st_drop_geometry() %>%
  transmute(
    weights,
    area = units::set_units(area, "km^2"),
    area_low = units::set_units(area_low, "km^2"),
    area_high = units::set_units(area_high, "km^2")
  )
#> # A tibble: 2 × 4
#>   weights    area area_low area_high
#>   <chr>    [km^2]   [km^2]    [km^2]
#> 1 uniform    756.     430.     1175.
#> 2 weighted   760.     432.     1182.

Note that the table of models includes all buffalo: hr_tt_akde() matches the models to the tracks by their id. Here, weighting changes the estimated area only slightly, but it changes the shape of the home range, as we can see by plotting the two isopleths over the track of Pepper:

ggplot() +
  geom_track_path(data = pepper_tt, colour = "grey50", linewidth = 0.1) +
  geom_sf(
    data = pepper_iso,
    mapping = aes(colour = weights),
    fill = NA,
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(31.6, 32, by = 0.1)) +
  labs(colour = "Weights")

Comparing home ranges

As the UDs of all buffalo are on the same grid, we can compute their overlap with hr_tt_ud_overlap(). With method = "ba", the overlap is measured by the Bhattacharyya coefficient, which is 1 for identical UDs and 0 for UDs that share no area:

buffalo_ba <- hr_tt_ud_overlap(buffalo_akde, method = "ba")
buffalo_ba
#>            Cilla      Gabs     Mvubu Pepper
#> Cilla  1.0000000 0.9424306 0.9776695      0
#> Gabs   0.9424306 1.0000000 0.9125376      0
#> Mvubu  0.9776695 0.9125376 1.0000000      0
#> Pepper 0.0000000 0.0000000 0.0000000      1

Alternatively, we can use ctmm::overlap() on the ctmm UDs, which also estimates the Bhattacharyya coefficient, with confidence intervals:

buffalo_overlap <- ctmm::overlap(buffalo_akde$ud_ctmm)

The element CI of the result is an array with the lower bound, the estimate and the upper bound of the overlap of each pair of buffalo. For Cilla and Gabs, we get:

buffalo_overlap$CI["Cilla", "Gabs", ]
#>       low       est      high 
#> 0.8958166 0.9958137 1.0000000

The estimate of ctmm (0.996) is higher than the overlap computed by hr_tt_ud_overlap() (0.942), because ctmm corrects it for a bias (Winner et al. 2018). Each UD is estimated from few independent observations of the home range (dof_area is only 4.3 for Gabs), so even two buffalo using exactly the same area would have estimated UDs that differ by chance: the overlap of the estimated UDs, as computed by hr_tt_ud_overlap(), underestimates the overlap of the true UDs. ctmm uses the movement models to estimate how large this bias is, and removes it (with debias = FALSE, it gives the same estimate as hr_tt_ud_overlap()). Here, nearly all the difference between the UDs of Cilla and Gabs could be due to chance, so the corrected estimate is close to 1. This does not mean that the two buffalo use exactly the same area, but that we cannot tell their home ranges apart with these data: the confidence interval shows that their overlap is at least 0.896.

The ctmm UDs can also be used for population-level analyses, such as estimating the mean home range area of the buffalo with ctmm::meta():

ctmm::meta(buffalo_akde$ud_ctmm)
#>                     ΔAICc
#> Dirac-δ          0.000000
#> inverse-Gaussian 9.323209

#>                 low      est     high
#> mean (km²) 372.0995 498.3215 642.6934
#> CoV²         0.0000   0.0000      Inf
#> CoV          0.0000   0.0000      Inf

Population home ranges

The home ranges of several individuals can be combined into a population home range with hr_tt_akde_pop(). By default, it uses population kernel density estimation (ctmm::pkde()), which estimates the population UD from the locations of all the individuals, using the movement model of each of them; it therefore needs the tibble of tracks and the table of models, as well as the UDs. The uncertainty of the population home range area accounts for the variation among individuals, so it can be large when combining few individuals.

Population kernel density estimation assumes that the individuals are a sample from a single population, sharing an area. Cilla, Gabs and Mvubu live in the same area in the south of the park, whereas Pepper lives further north, so we combine the home ranges of the three southern buffalo. Combining at least three individuals is also safer: with only two, the parameters of the population are poorly determined, and their estimation can fail. ctmm estimates some of these parameters (e.g. the bandwidth of the population kernels) with a stochastic optimiser, so the results can differ between runs; to make them reproducible, we set the seed of the random number generator first:

south_ids <- c("Cilla", "Gabs", "Mvubu")
south_akde <- filter(buffalo_akde, buffalo_id %in% south_ids)
set.seed(1)
south_pop <- hr_tt_akde_pop(
  south_akde,
  tracks = buffalo_tt,
  models = buffalo_fit,
  levels = 0.95
)

As for the individual home ranges, we display the area of the population home range, with its confidence interval:

south_pop %>%
  sf::st_drop_geometry() %>%
  transmute(
    method,
    n_ud,
    area = units::set_units(area, "km^2"),
    area_low = units::set_units(area_low, "km^2"),
    area_high = units::set_units(area_high, "km^2")
  )
#> # A tibble: 1 × 5
#>   method  n_ud   area area_low area_high
#>   <chr>  <int> [km^2]   [km^2]    [km^2]
#> 1 pkde       3   377.     261.      516.
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(
    data = filter(buffalo_iso, level == 0.95, buffalo_id %in% south_ids),
    mapping = aes(colour = buffalo_id),
    fill = NA
  ) +
  geom_sf(data = south_pop, fill = "grey50", alpha = 0.3) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(31.8, 32, by = 0.1)) +
  labs(colour = "Buffalo")

Alternatively, with method = "mean", the population UD is the average of the individual UDs (as with hr_tt_ud_sum()), with confidence intervals of the population home range area. If the table of UDs is grouped (e.g. after joining a variable from the metadata, such as sex, and grouping by it), a population home range is estimated for each group.

Going further

The fitted models can be used with any other function of ctmm, by combining them with the telemetry objects created with mt_as_telemetry(). For example, we can estimate the mean speed of Cilla, with its confidence interval:

cilla_speed <- ctmm::speed(
  buffalo_fit$model$Cilla,
  buffalo_tel$Cilla,
  trace = FALSE
)
cilla_speed
#> $DOF
#>    speed 
#> 2981.384 
#> 
#> $CI
#>                             low      est     high
#> speed (kilometers/day) 10.94474 11.14431 11.34477
#> 
#> attr(,"class")
#> [1] "speed"

The mean speed of Cilla (11.1 km/day) is lower than the speed in the summary of its model (14.1 km/day, see above), which is the root-mean-square speed: the square root of the mean of the squared speeds, which gives more weight to fast movements.

We can also simulate a track from the model of Cilla, conditional on the observed locations (e.g. to fill gaps), and convert it back to a tibble of tracks with mt_as_move2():

# times every 20 minutes during the first two days of the track
cilla_times <- seq(
  from = min(buffalo_tel$Cilla$t),
  to = min(buffalo_tel$Cilla$t) + 2 %#% "day",
  by = 20 %#% "minute"
)
cilla_sim <- simulate(
  buffalo_fit$model$Cilla,
  data = buffalo_tel$Cilla,
  t = cilla_times
)
# simulated tracks only have the time in seconds, so we add the timestamp
cilla_sim$timestamp <- as.POSIXct(
  cilla_sim$t,
  origin = "1970-01-01",
  tz = "UTC"
)
cilla_sim_tt <- mt_as_move2(cilla_sim)
cilla_sim_tt
